title: Crowe wasn't 'hog-tied'
article: --- While witnesses maintain a Regina man who died in an ambulance after being pepper sprayed and sedated was never "hog-tied," two police officers agree he had handcuff-like bruises on his ankles.
"That does look similar to the indentations left by handcuffs," Regina police Staff Sgt. Murray Roe testified Friday at a coroner's inquest when shown autopsy photos of Vernon Dale Crowe.
Similarly, RCMP Staff Sgt. Sandy Ervin said, "I've seen marks like that that have been left by handcuffs."
Hog-tying is shackling a prisoner's hands and feet behind his back with the two restraints pulled together, forcing the legs upwards.
The six-person jury has heard an officer bound Crowe's feet with gauze bandage while he lay on his stomach with his hands cuffed in the back. The two restraints weren't connected, he said.
Roe and Ervin, experts in use of force, said binding a prisoner's hands and feet without connecting the two restraints would not be considered hog-tying -- a practice which has fallen out of favour.
"It reduces the person's ability to breathe," Roe explained.
"I don't believe it's illegal ... It's discouraged to be used," Roe said in response to questions from Crowe family lawyer Darren Winegarden who raised the issue.

Crowe died July 10, 2001, about a half hour after suffering an epileptic seizure inside Souls Harbour Mission, 1762 Broad St. The seizure was over when the 32-year-old climbed into an ambulance at 5:31 p.m., but he agreed to be checked out anyway.
At 5:33 p.m. paramedic Jason Williams called for police help when Crowe suddenly became combative. Two more calls -- including a distress code -- followed.
When Const. Dean Ross arrived around 5:37 p.m., he joined the struggle. Ross grabbed Crowe's hair, once pushed his head back with the heel of his hand, and put his knee on Crowe's shoulder.
Both witnesses said they didn't believe Crowe was deliberately fighting, but appeared to be suffering a medical problem.

In his thrashing, Crowe "dragged his teeth" across the officer's forearm and struck the officer head-to-head. Ross reacted by pepper spraying Crowe, who was still wrestling despite being handcuffed in the front.
Both Roe and Ervin said in their opinion, Ross, a fellow police officer, acted appropriately.

Despite the pepper spray, Crowe continued to struggle. Williams sedated him, but the drug isn't effective for 10 to 12 minutes. Seconds after the injection, Ross stepped aside when three additional paramedics and four police officers arrived.
Ten minutes later, Crowe -- lying on his stomach, his hands cuffed behind his back, and legs bound -- became docile. Paramedics realized he had no pulse.
Questions have been raised about the prone position in which Crowe was placed. Both Roe and Ervin said the position is standard to control a prisoner, although it does restrict breathing.
After Crowe's death, the Regina Police Service began making its officers aware of "positional asphyxia" and "excited delirium."
Roe said the relatively new terms have been connected to prisoners developing breathing difficulties or an elevated heartbeat and dying.
Both officers agreed hog-tying a prisoner could worsen those problems.
The inquest continues Tuesday when medical experts are expected to testify.
